screens.title: Python for Network Automation Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will gain practical, lab-ready skills for using Python to interact with Cisco devices. We begin by establishing a clean development environment using virtual environments, then install the libraries you need, and move through real examples that connect to devices, run show commands, and push configuration safely. You will see how netmiko, a higher-level library built on paramiko, reduces the boilerplate for SSH-based automation and makes common tasks like sending commands and applying configuration lists straightforward. Along the way we emphasize practical safeguards: avoid hardcoding credentials, use try/except blocks for typical connection failures, and use Python's logging module instead of print statements so your scripts are auditable. There is a brief hands-on activity included: a gather-and-save script that connects to multiple devices, collects command outputs, and writes them to files. By the end of this chapter you will understand the main library primitives, be able to prototype simple automation scripts in a lab, and know the most common pitfalls to avoid before moving into production.

Python for Network Automation Fundamentals

Practical steps to create a reproducible Python environment, connect via SSH using netmiko, run show commands, push configuration, and add error handling and logging.

In this lesson

Set up virtual environments, install netmiko, and write scripts to retrieve and push device configurations while handling errors and logging.

Who it's for

Network engineers preparing for lab automation tasks and CCIE-level scripting who need reliable SSH automation workflows.

What you'll build

A netmiko-based script that gathers show outputs, applies a simple loopback config, verifies it, and saves logs and files.

Cautions

Avoid hardcoding credentials, always test in a lab, and save running-config to startup-config when making persistent changes.

Concept map
Virtual environment
Isolate dependencies for safe automation development.
Netmiko / Paramiko
SSH libraries for device connections and command execution.
Scripts & Logging
Use logging and error handling to make scripts safe and auditable.
Explore Key Topics
Virtual Environments
Create isolated projects to avoid dependency conflicts and keep your automation reproducible.
Netmiko Basics
Use ConnectHandler, send_command, and send_config_set to perform CLI automation with less boilerplate than paramiko.
Errors & Logging
Handle authentication and timeout exceptions and log events to a file for reliable troubleshooting.

screens.title: Virtual Environments — why and how
screens.narratorSegment: A virtual environment creates an isolated Python runtime and package directory for a single project. This prevents one project's dependency versions from conflicting with another's or the system Python. For network automation you will often use libraries like netmiko, paramiko, and logging utilities; isolating them in a virtual environment makes your scripts reproducible and prevents accidental upgrades to shared system packages. To create a venv, run Python three -m venv followed by the directory name, for example Python three -m venv netauto_env. Activate it with the platform-appropriate command shown in the examples. Once it's active your prompt usually shows the venv name and pip install will only affect that environment. A common mistake is to skip the venv and install packages globally; that creates hard-to-diagnose version mismatches on other machines or CI systems. Another misconception is that virtual environments are only for web apps — they are essential for any Python automation project. As a practical step, after activation install netmiko and test import by running a tiny script that imports ConnectHandler. If the import fails, check pip list inside the venv. The core takeaway: always start automation projects inside a dedicated virtual environment so your lab and production deployments remain predictable.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Virtual Environments
Definition & Why it matters

A virtual environment isolates project packages from the system Python. In network automation this isolation ensures that netmiko or parsing libraries you install for one lab do not break other projects or global tooling.

Common mistake
Installing netmiko globally leads to version drift and fragile reproducibility when moving scripts between machines.
Pro tip
Record dependencies with pip freeze > requirements.txt to recreate the environment precisely on another lab machine.
Quick commands
# Create a virtual environment named 'netauto_env'
python3 -m venv netauto_env

# Activate the virtual environment (Linux/macOS)
source netauto_env/bin/activate

# Activate on Windows (Command Prompt)
netauto_env\Scripts\activate.bat

# Activate on Windows (PowerShell)
netauto_env\Scripts\Activate.ps1

# Install netmiko inside the venv
pip install netmiko
Example
After activation, run python -c "import netmiko; print('ok')" to verify the package is available in that environment.
Key Takeaway

Use virtual environments for every automation project to keep dependencies predictable and reproducible across labs and CI.

screens.title: Install and verify netmiko
screens.narratorSegment: Installing netmiko inside an activated virtual environment is straightforward but it's important to follow the steps and verify the result. First activate the venv so pip targets only that environment. Then run pip install netmiko. After installation, confirm success by listing installed packages with pip list or by running python and importing the library. A practical verification is writing a tiny one-line check that imports ConnectHandler and prints a short confirmation. One common pitfall is using the system pip rather than the environment's pip; using the venv's pip avoids this. Another is forgetting to activate PowerShell's execution policy on Windows, which prevents activation scripts — in that case use the PowerShell activation command provided. When working in teams, capture exact versions with pip freeze and commit a requirements. txt so others can reproduce the same runtime. Finally, install any parsing libraries you plan to use, like TextFSM or genie, only after confirming netmiko works. That keeps the initial troubleshooting focused on the SSH layer before adding parsing complexity. Install and verify netmiko means activate venv, pip install netmiko, run a simple import test, and freeze versions to requirements.txt for reproducibility.. In practical terms, steps to add netmiko to your project and confirm it's importable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Install & Verify
Step-by-step
  1. Activate your virtual environment so pip targets it.
  2. Run pip install netmiko inside the activated venv.
  3. Verify with pip list or run a one-line import test in python.
  4. Capture versions with pip freeze > requirements.txt for reproducibility.
Pro tip
Test import in the same shell where you activated the venv to confirm the environment is active.
Common mistake
Using system python or pip by accident; the installed package won’t be available inside your venv shell.
Command examples
# Inside your activated virtual environment
pip install netmiko

# Quick import check
python -c "from netmiko import ConnectHandler; print('netmiko ok')"

# Freeze versions
pip freeze > requirements.txt
Key Takeaway

Install netmiko in the active venv and verify the package is importable before proceeding to device connections.

screens.title: paramiko vs netmiko
screens.narratorSegment: Paramiko is a low-level SSHv2 implementation that gives you fine control over SSH sessions, key exchanges, and low-level transport. It is useful when you need custom SSH behavior or to implement an SSH server or unusual authentication method. Netmiko sits on top of paramiko and intentionally simplifies common network automation tasks: it abstracts device-specific prompts, handles paging, and provides convenient methods like send_command and send_config_set that accept lists of configuration lines. For everyday CLI automation against Cisco IOS, IOS XE, NX-OS, and many other vendors, netmiko reduces code complexity and speeds development. A common misconception is that netmiko replaces paramiko entirely — rather, netmiko uses paramiko and adds the device CLI handling layer. Choose paramiko if you need raw SSH control or specialized transport features; choose netmiko for scripted CLI operations in labs or production where prompt handling and pagination are the primary concerns. In practice, start with netmiko for device tasks and only fall back to paramiko when you need a custom transport or server behavior. This saves development time while keeping the option to dive deeper if necessary.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › paramiko vs netmiko
Paramiko (low-level)
  • Implements SSHv2 transport and channels.
  • Gives raw control over authentication and key exchange.
  • Requires manual handling of CLI prompts, pagination, and send/receive loops.
Use when
You need custom SSH behavior or to implement an SSH server or nonstandard transport.
Netmiko (higher-level)
  • Built on paramiko, but handles device CLI differences and pagination.
  • Provides ConnectHandler, send_command, and send_config_set helpers.
  • Simplifies multi-vendor CLI automation workflows.
Use when
You need to run show commands or push configurations across standard network devices efficiently.
Misconception
Netmiko is not a separate protocol; it reuses paramiko for SSH transport.
Practical tip
Start with netmiko for CLI scripts; keep paramiko knowledge if you need custom SSH control later.
Example
Use netmiko's send_config_set to push a list of interface commands without manual prompt handling.

screens.title: ConnectHandler — establish an SSH session
screens.narratorSegment: ConnectHandler is netmiko's main convenience class for establishing and managing SSH connections to devices. You provide a dictionary with keys like device_type, host, username, password, port, and optionally secret for privileged mode. The library handles opening the SSH session and typical CLI quirks. In practice you should avoid hardcoding credentials; use environment variables or a secure vault. The example in this chapter shows a typical pattern: create the device dict, open a context manager with ConnectHandler so the connection closes automatically, send a show command with send_command, and print or capture the output. A common misuse is to open many simultaneous connections without closing them—using a context manager with with ConnectHandler(**device) as net_connect prevents that. Also be mindful of device_type: use the correct string for the platform, such as cisco_ios or cisco_xe for IOS XE. Finally always validate the returned output before parsing; raw CLI can include banners or paging prompts. This walkthrough prepares you to run show and config commands reliably in subsequent screens. ConnectHandler — establish an SSH session means use a device dict, prefer environment variables for credentials, and use a with-context to automatically close connections.. In practical terms, use a device dictionary to connect and run a show command. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › ConnectHandler
Pattern explanation

The ConnectHandler context manager opens and closes connections cleanly, avoiding resource leaks. The device dictionary centralizes parameters and can reference environment variables for credentials to improve security.

Common misconception
Closing a connection manually is error-prone; prefer the with-context so connections close even when exceptions occur.
Code (safe pattern)
from netmiko import ConnectHandler
import os

device = {
  "device_type": "cisco_ios",
  "host": os.getenv("NET_HOST", "192.168.1.1"),
  "username": os.getenv("NET_USERNAME", "admin"),
  "password": os.getenv("NET_PASSWORD", "cisco"),
  "port": 22,
  "secret": os.getenv("NET_SECRET", "enable_password"),
}

with ConnectHandler(**device) as net_connect:
  output = net_connect.send_command("show ip interface brief")
  print(output)
Example
Use environment variables to avoid committing credentials to source control.
Check
Validate host reachability before attempting many connections to speed troubleshooting.
Tip
Use net_connect.find_prompt() to confirm you're in the expected CLI mode before sending config commands.

screens.title: Running show commands and collecting output
screens.narratorSegment: Show commands are safe first steps when building automation because they are read-only and let you validate connectivity and parsing strategies. Netmiko's send_command method runs a single show command and returns the device's raw CLI output as a string. For collecting inventory or troubleshooting data, run show version and show ip interface brief and write outputs to disk. When you run multiple commands, loop through a list of commands and save each response to a separate file named with the device identifier and command name. One practical tip is to normalize filenames by replacing spaces with underscores. Be aware that raw CLI output can include pagination or banners; netmiko handles paging for you, but always inspect the output for unexpected login messages. If you intend to parse output programmatically later, store the raw text as a canonical copy and use parsing libraries like TextFSM or genie in a separate parsing step. This layered approach—collect raw text, then parse—lets you re-run parsers without reconnecting to devices, simplifying debugging and audits. Running show commands and collecting output means gather raw show outputs into files first; parse them later with dedicated parsers so collection and parsing are decoupled.. In practical terms, use send_command and save outputs for audits and parsing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Collecting Output
Why collect raw output

Storing raw command output creates an auditable record and lets you iterate on parsing without reconnecting to devices. It's a robust practice for inventory and troubleshooting workflows.

Best practice
Name files consistently and keep raw outputs immutable. Parse in a separate step using a parser library so errors in parsing don't require a fresh device connection.
Example loop
commands = ["show version", "show ip interface brief"]
for cmd in commands:
  output = net_connect.send_command(cmd)
  filename = f"{device_name}_{cmd.replace(' ', '_')}.txt"
  with open(filename, "w") as f:
    f.write(output)
Common issue
Parsing raw CLI directly in the connection loop couples collection and parsing and makes retries awkward.
Pro tip
Save raw files, then write a separate parser script using TextFSM or genie to convert text to structured data.
Verification
After collecting, open one file to confirm output completeness and absence of unexpected banners.

screens.title: Applying configuration with send_config_set
screens.narratorSegment: Sending configuration lines to a device is a step that changes state and therefore requires extra care. Netmiko's send_config_set accepts a list of configuration commands and applies them in configuration mode, handling the enter and exit of the mode for you. A safe workflow is: first run show commands to confirm existing state, prepare a small list of config lines, call send_config_set, then run a verification show run for the specific interface or feature you changed. After verifying, remember to persist the change with write memory or use netmiko's save_config helper where available. A frequent mistake is assuming changes are persistent; without explicitly saving the running-config to startup-config, a device reload will lose them. Also avoid sending large bulk changes without testing in a lab. Use short, idempotent configuration commands—those that can be applied multiple times without changing the final state—to reduce unintended side effects. Finally, run verification commands programmatically and record both the apply output and the verification output to logs so you can audit what changed and when. Applying configuration with send_config_set means apply config with send_config_set, verify with targeted show run output, then issue write memory to persist changes.. In practical terms, push a list of configuration lines and verify persistence. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Apply Configuration
Safe apply workflow
  1. Collect current state with show commands.
  2. Prepare a concise, idempotent list of config lines.
  3. Apply with send_config_set and capture the output.
  4. Verify with a targeted show run command for the changed object.
  5. Persist with write memory or a save function.
Common mistake
Forgetting to save to startup-config so changes are lost after a reboot.
Code example
config_commands = [
  "interface Loopback100",
  "description Test Loopback from Netmiko",
  "ip address 10.10.10.1 255.255.255.255",
  "no shutdown"
]
output = net_connect.send_config_set(config_commands)
print(output)
# Verify
verify_output = net_connect.send_command("show run interface Loopback100")
print(verify_output)
# Save
net_connect.send_command("write memory")
Idempotency
Design config commands so re-applying them has no further effect to avoid drift.
Audit
Log both the apply output and verification output so you can trace what changed.
Lab tip
Test changes on a single device or virtual lab before scaling to many devices.

screens.title: Error handling — exceptions you must catch
screens.narratorSegment: Error handling is essential for automation resilience. Netmiko raises specific exceptions when connections fail or authentication is rejected. Two common exceptions are NetmikoTimeoutException for unreachable devices and NetmikoAuthenticationException for bad credentials. Your scripts should catch these specific exceptions and log a clear message, then either retry or skip the device depending on your policy. Use a try/except/finally structure where the finally block ensures cleanup or journaling steps run even when an error occurs. Avoid broad except statements that swallow errors without recording them — they make debugging harder. In addition to handling netmiko exceptions, catch generic exceptions at a higher level to capture unexpected failures and log tracebacks. For long runs across many devices, record both successful and failed device attempts to a log file so you can retry later. This chapter demonstrates catching the named netmiko exceptions and using logging. error or logging. critical to preserve stack traces for post-mortem analysis. Proper error handling turns unpredictable automation into an auditable process you can operate safely in labs and production. In practical terms, use try/except/finally and handle netmiko-specific exceptions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Error Handling
Exceptions to plan for
  • NetmikoAuthenticationException — bad username/password.
  • NetmikoTimeoutException — device unreachable or SSH port blocked.
  • Generic exceptions for unexpected failures that should be logged with traceback.
Misconception
Catching Exception without logging makes it difficult to troubleshoot intermittent failures.
Error handling pattern
from netmiko import ConnectHandler, NetmikoAuthenticationException, NetmikoTimeoutException
import logging

try:
  logging.info(f"Attempting to connect to {device['host']}")
  with ConnectHandler(**device) as net_connect:
    logging.info("Successfully connected")
    # send commands
except NetmikoAuthenticationException:
  logging.error("Authentication failed for device")
except NetmikoTimeoutException:
  logging.error("Connection timed out for device")
except Exception as e:
  logging.critical(f"Unexpected error: {e}", exc_info=True)
finally:
  logging.info("Completed attempt for device")
Retry policy
Decide whether to retry after timeouts or to log and continue; implement exponential backoff if retrying.
Auditability
Log errors with context: device, attempted command, timestamps, and stack traces when appropriate.
Lab tip
Introduce a test device that intentionally fails to exercise your exception handling paths safely.

screens.title: Logging — replace prints with structured logs
screens.narratorSegment: Replace ad-hoc print statements with Python's built-in logging module to create reliable, timestamped records of automation runs. Configure logging at the start of your script with logging. basicConfig to set filename, level, and message format so every run appends to a log file. Use logging. info for progress messages, logging. error for recoverable failures, and logging. critical for unexpected exceptions that include stack traces. This structured approach makes logs searchable and integrates with centralized log collectors if you move beyond a single machine. In a multi-device run, log each device attempt with the device identifier, the commands you sent, and the outcome. That way you can re-run only failed devices later. Logs also let you separate human-facing console output from machine-readable logs. A common mistake is leaving debug-level logs on in production; set the appropriate log level and consider rotating logs or using a logging handler that rolls files by size or date. Thoughtful logging transforms scripts from one-off experiments into maintainable automation tools you can audit and operate safely. In practical terms, use python's logging module for auditable automation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Logging
Why logging matters

Logs provide timestamps, context, and severity levels so you can audit runs, debug failures, and operate automation at scale. They are essential for reliable maintenance and incident response.

Recommendation
Log device attempts, commands sent, verification results, and exception stack traces. Keep logs separate from user-facing console prints.
Logging template
import logging

logging.basicConfig(
  filename='netauto.log',
  level=logging.INFO,
  format='%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s'
)

logging.info(f"Attempting to connect to {device['host']}")
Rotation
Use rotating file handlers if your automation produces large logs over time.
Context
Include device hostnames or IPs and command identifiers in each log entry for later filtering.
Debugging
Reserve debug logs for development; avoid verbose logs in production runs unless troubleshooting.

screens.title: Security considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Security must be a first-class concern when your scripts access network devices. Never hardcode usernames or passwords directly in scripts that may be committed to version control. Instead, use environment variables accessed via os. getenv or a dedicated secret store. The examples show using os. getenv to fall back to defaults for lab convenience, but in production you should integrate with a secret manager. Also consider SSH host key verification to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks; netmiko supports safe SSH handling, and you should not disable host key checks in production. Another area to watch is privilege escalation: if a script needs enable mode, supply the secret parameter and ensure the automation user has the appropriate rights without giving unnecessary privileges. The chapter also notes idempotency: write configuration commands so repeated application does not produce different results, which reduces the risk of accidental state changes. Finally, test automation in a segregated lab before production and audit logs to detect unexpected actions. Following these practices helps ensure automation is both effective and safe. Security considerations means use environment variables or secret stores for credentials, enable host key verification, and design idempotent config changes to reduce risk.. In practical terms, avoid hardcoded credentials, use environment variables, and enable host key verification. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Security
Key security practices
  • Never hardcode credentials; use os.getenv or a secret manager.
  • Enable SSH host key verification to avoid MITM risks.
  • Grant minimal privileges needed for automation users and use enable secrets when required.
  • Test in lab and audit logs before production use.
Common mistake
Hardcoding credentials into scripts and committing them to source control exposes devices to compromise.
Environment variable example
import os
host = os.getenv("NET_HOST")
username = os.getenv("NET_USERNAME")
password = os.getenv("NET_PASSWORD")
For production, replace environment variables with a secure vault and control access explicitly.
Why it matters

Secure credential handling and SSH verification prevent unauthorized access and ensure your automation is trustworthy.

screens.title: Parsing CLI output — plan for structure
screens.narratorSegment: Parsing unstructured CLI output is brittle if done ad-hoc. The recommended pattern is to gather raw output first and then parse it using a dedicated parsing tool. TextFSM and genie are libraries designed to convert command text into structured data, but their use is separate from collection. By decoupling collection and parsing, you can retain raw evidence and iterate on parsing rules without reconnecting to devices. Start by saving the output of show commands into files with predictable names and formats. Then build a parser script that consumes those files and outputs structured objects like lists or dictionaries. This separation helps when outputs vary slightly across platform versions or device models because you can improve the parser without touching the collection step. A common misconception is that send_command returns structured data — it returns raw text. Treat that text as the canonical artifact. Use tests on sample output files to validate parsers before integrating them into automation that drives decisions. This approach reduces errors and keeps your automation auditable and maintainable. In practical terms, store raw text and parse later with textfsm or genie for reliable automation. Why separate collection and parsing

Separating these steps makes debugging and parser development easier. You can tweak parsing rules on stored files without reconnecting to devices or re-running collection jobs.

Practical workflow
  1. Collect raw output files named predictably.
  2. Develop parser(s) against sample files in a separate script.
  3. Validate parser outputs against expected keys and types.
  4. Integrate parsing into reporting pipelines once stable.
Practical note
TextFSM and genie will be addressed in later chapters; for now, store clean raw outputs and design file names that include device and command.
Example filename
R1_show_version.txt or 192.168.1.101_show_ip_interface_brief.txt
Key Takeaway

Collect raw CLI text first. Parse later with dedicated libraries to make your automation maintainable and testable.

screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks you through a starter script that connects to multiple devices, runs a set of show commands, and saves each output to files. content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › gather_info.py
Activity Goals
  • Connect to multiple devices using netmiko.
  • Collect a set of show commands and save outputs to files.
  • Log successes and failures for auditability.
Try this
Add show cdp neighbors detail to the commands_to_gather list and confirm the corresponding file is created for each reachable device.
Starter template
from netmiko import ConnectHandler, NetmikoAuthenticationException, NetmikoTimeoutException
import logging
import os

logging.basicConfig(filename="device_info.log", level=logging.INFO,
                    format="%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s")

devices = [
  {"device_type": "cisco_ios", "host": "192.168.1.101", "username": "admin", "password": "cisco", "secret": "enable_password"},
  {"device_type": "cisco_ios", "host": "192.168.1.102", "username": "admin", "password": "cisco", "secret": "enable_password"}
]

commands_to_gather = ["show version", "show ip interface brief", "show cdp neighbors detail"]

output_dir = "device_outputs"
if not os.path.exists(output_dir):
  os.makedirs(output_dir)

for device in devices:
  device_name = device["host"]
  logging.info(f"Attempting to connect to {device_name}")
  try:
    with ConnectHandler(**device) as net_connect:
      logging.info(f"Connected to {device_name}")
      for cmd in commands_to_gather:
        output = net_connect.send_command(cmd)
        filename = f"{output_dir}/{device_name}_{cmd.replace(' ', '_')}.txt"
        with open(filename, "w") as f:
          f.write(output)
        logging.info(f"Saved output of '{cmd}' for {device_name} to {filename}")
  except NetmikoAuthenticationException:
    logging.error(f"Authentication failed for {device_name}")
  except NetmikoTimeoutException:
    logging.error(f"Connection timed out for {device_name}")
  except Exception as e:
    logging.critical(f"Unexpected error for {device_name}: {e}", exc_info=True)

logging.info("Script finished.")
Key Takeaway

This activity produces raw evidence and logs. Use it as a scaffold to add parsing, credential sources, and retries later.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will gain practical, lab-ready skills for using Python to interact with Cisco devices. We begin by establishing a clean development environment using virtual environments, then install the libraries you need, and move through real examples that connect to devices, run show commands, and push configuration safely. You will see how netmiko, a higher-level library built on paramiko, reduces the boilerplate for SSH-based automation and makes common tasks like sending commands and applying configuration lists straightforward. Along the way we emphasize practical safeguards: avoid hardcoding credentials, use try/except blocks for typical connection failures, and use Python's logging module instead of print statements so your scripts are auditable. There is a brief hands-on activity included: a gather-and-save script that connects to multiple devices, collects command outputs, and writes them to files. By the end of this chapter you will understand the main library primitives, be able to prototype simple automation scripts in a lab, and know the most common pitfalls to avoid before moving into production.

These four objectives guide your practical progress through Python-based network automation. First, you'll set up a dedicated Python environment to avoid dependency conflicts and make your projects reproducible. I will show you how to create and activate a virtual environment across common platforms. Second, you will learn to use SSH libraries: paramiko at a low level and netmiko as a convenience layer. You'll understand when to prefer netmiko for device CLI automation. Third, you'll write scripts that connect to devices, retrieve show command output, and push simple configuration sets, with concrete code templates you can run in a lab. Finally, you'll implement basic error handling and logging so scripts are resilient and auditable. Each objective pairs a practical task with a verification milestone you can check in your lab. Throughout, we'll emphasize secure practices like using environment variables for credentials rather than hardcoding them. By the time you finish, you'll have runnable starter scripts and the competence to expand them safely into fuller automation solutions.

This slide maps each objective to a concrete verification task you can run in a lab. For environment setup, create a virtual environment using the provided python command and activate it; then install netmiko and list installed packages to confirm isolation. For SSH libraries, write a short script that imports paramiko and netmiko; try a local SSH test or mock to see if the imports succeed. For scripting, use the included ConnectHandler template: connect to a lab device, run a show command, and capture the output to a file. Confirm you can apply a small configuration such as creating a loopback, run a verification command, and then issue write memory to persist it. For errors and logging, intentionally supply a bad credential to trigger an authentication exception and verify your script catches it and logs a helpful message. These hands-on checks ensure you don’t just read the examples, you can run them and interpret failures safely.

A virtual environment creates an isolated Python runtime and package directory for a single project. This prevents one project's dependency versions from conflicting with another's or the system Python. For network automation you will often use libraries like netmiko, paramiko, and logging utilities; isolating them in a virtual environment makes your scripts reproducible and prevents accidental upgrades to shared system packages. To create a venv, run Python three -m venv followed by the directory name, for example Python three -m venv netauto_env. Activate it with the platform-appropriate command shown in the examples. Once it's active your prompt usually shows the venv name and pip install will only affect that environment. A common mistake is to skip the venv and install packages globally; that creates hard-to-diagnose version mismatches on other machines or CI systems. Another misconception is that virtual environments are only for web apps — they are essential for any Python automation project. As a practical step, after activation install netmiko and test import by running a tiny script that imports ConnectHandler. If the import fails, check pip list inside the venv. The core takeaway: always start automation projects inside a dedicated virtual environment so your lab and production deployments remain predictable.

Installing netmiko inside an activated virtual environment is straightforward but it's important to follow the steps and verify the result. First activate the venv so pip targets only that environment. Then run pip install netmiko. After installation, confirm success by listing installed packages with pip list or by running python and importing the library. A practical verification is writing a tiny one-line check that imports ConnectHandler and prints a short confirmation. One common pitfall is using the system pip rather than the environment's pip; using the venv's pip avoids this. Another is forgetting to activate PowerShell's execution policy on Windows, which prevents activation scripts — in that case use the PowerShell activation command provided. When working in teams, capture exact versions with pip freeze and commit a requirements. txt so others can reproduce the same runtime. Finally, install any parsing libraries you plan to use, like TextFSM or genie, only after confirming netmiko works. That keeps the initial troubleshooting focused on the SSH layer before adding parsing complexity. Paramiko is a low-level SSHv2 implementation that gives you fine control over SSH sessions, key exchanges, and low-level transport. It is useful when you need custom SSH behavior or to implement an SSH server or unusual authentication method. Netmiko sits on top of paramiko and intentionally simplifies common network automation tasks: it abstracts device-specific prompts, handles paging, and provides convenient methods like send_command and send_config_set that accept lists of configuration lines. For everyday CLI automation against Cisco IOS, IOS XE, NX-OS, and many other vendors, netmiko reduces code complexity and speeds development. A common misconception is that netmiko replaces paramiko entirely — rather, netmiko uses paramiko and adds the device CLI handling layer. Choose paramiko if you need raw SSH control or specialized transport features; choose netmiko for scripted CLI operations in labs or production where prompt handling and pagination are the primary concerns. In practice, start with netmiko for device tasks and only fall back to paramiko when you need a custom transport or server behavior. This saves development time while keeping the option to dive deeper if necessary.

ConnectHandler is netmiko's main convenience class for establishing and managing SSH connections to devices. You provide a dictionary with keys like device_type, host, username, password, port, and optionally secret for privileged mode. The library handles opening the SSH session and typical CLI quirks. In practice you should avoid hardcoding credentials; use environment variables or a secure vault. The example in this chapter shows a typical pattern: create the device dict, open a context manager with ConnectHandler so the connection closes automatically, send a show command with send_command, and print or capture the output. A common misuse is to open many simultaneous connections without closing them—using a context manager with with ConnectHandler(**device) as net_connect prevents that. Also be mindful of device_type: use the correct string for the platform, such as cisco_ios or cisco_xe for IOS XE. Finally always validate the returned output before parsing; raw CLI can include banners or paging prompts. This walkthrough prepares you to run show and config commands reliably in subsequent screens. Show commands are safe first steps when building automation because they are read-only and let you validate connectivity and parsing strategies. Netmiko's send_command method runs a single show command and returns the device's raw CLI output as a string. For collecting inventory or troubleshooting data, run show version and show ip interface brief and write outputs to disk. When you run multiple commands, loop through a list of commands and save each response to a separate file named with the device identifier and command name. One practical tip is to normalize filenames by replacing spaces with underscores. Be aware that raw CLI output can include pagination or banners; netmiko handles paging for you, but always inspect the output for unexpected login messages. If you intend to parse output programmatically later, store the raw text as a canonical copy and use parsing libraries like TextFSM or genie in a separate parsing step. This layered approach—collect raw text, then parse—lets you re-run parsers without reconnecting to devices, simplifying debugging and audits. Sending configuration lines to a device is a step that changes state and therefore requires extra care. Netmiko's send_config_set accepts a list of configuration commands and applies them in configuration mode, handling the enter and exit of the mode for you. A safe workflow is: first run show commands to confirm existing state, prepare a small list of config lines, call send_config_set, then run a verification show run for the specific interface or feature you changed. After verifying, remember to persist the change with write memory or use netmiko's save_config helper where available. A frequent mistake is assuming changes are persistent; without explicitly saving the running-config to startup-config, a device reload will lose them. Also avoid sending large bulk changes without testing in a lab. Use short, idempotent configuration commands—those that can be applied multiple times without changing the final state—to reduce unintended side effects. Finally, run verification commands programmatically and record both the apply output and the verification output to logs so you can audit what changed and when. Error handling is essential for automation resilience. Netmiko raises specific exceptions when connections fail or authentication is rejected. Two common exceptions are NetmikoTimeoutException for unreachable devices and NetmikoAuthenticationException for bad credentials. Your scripts should catch these specific exceptions and log a clear message, then either retry or skip the device depending on your policy. Use a try/except/finally structure where the finally block ensures cleanup or journaling steps run even when an error occurs. Avoid broad except statements that swallow errors without recording them — they make debugging harder. In addition to handling netmiko exceptions, catch generic exceptions at a higher level to capture unexpected failures and log tracebacks. For long runs across many devices, record both successful and failed device attempts to a log file so you can retry later. This chapter demonstrates catching the named netmiko exceptions and using logging. error or logging. critical to preserve stack traces for post-mortem analysis. Proper error handling turns unpredictable automation into an auditable process you can operate safely in labs and production. Replace ad-hoc print statements with Python's built-in logging module to create reliable, timestamped records of automation runs. Configure logging at the start of your script with logging. basicConfig to set filename, level, and message format so every run appends to a log file. Use logging. info for progress messages, logging. error for recoverable failures, and logging. critical for unexpected exceptions that include stack traces. This structured approach makes logs searchable and integrates with centralized log collectors if you move beyond a single machine. In a multi-device run, log each device attempt with the device identifier, the commands you sent, and the outcome. That way you can re-run only failed devices later. Logs also let you separate human-facing console output from machine-readable logs. A common mistake is leaving debug-level logs on in production; set the appropriate log level and consider rotating logs or using a logging handler that rolls files by size or date. Thoughtful logging transforms scripts from one-off experiments into maintainable automation tools you can audit and operate safely. Security must be a first-class concern when your scripts access network devices. Never hardcode usernames or passwords directly in scripts that may be committed to version control. Instead, use environment variables accessed via os. getenv or a dedicated secret store. The examples show using os. getenv to fall back to defaults for lab convenience, but in production you should integrate with a secret manager. Also consider SSH host key verification to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks; netmiko supports safe SSH handling, and you should not disable host key checks in production. Another area to watch is privilege escalation: if a script needs enable mode, supply the secret parameter and ensure the automation user has the appropriate rights without giving unnecessary privileges. The chapter also notes idempotency: write configuration commands so repeated application does not produce different results, which reduces the risk of accidental state changes. Finally, test automation in a segregated lab before production and audit logs to detect unexpected actions. Following these practices helps ensure automation is both effective and safe. Parsing unstructured CLI output is brittle if done ad-hoc. The recommended pattern is to gather raw output first and then parse it using a dedicated parsing tool. TextFSM and genie are libraries designed to convert command text into structured data, but their use is separate from collection. By decoupling collection and parsing, you can retain raw evidence and iterate on parsing rules without reconnecting to devices. Start by saving the output of show commands into files with predictable names and formats. Then build a parser script that consumes those files and outputs structured objects like lists or dictionaries. This separation helps when outputs vary slightly across platform versions or device models because you can improve the parser without touching the collection step. A common misconception is that send_command returns structured data — it returns raw text. Treat that text as the canonical artifact. Use tests on sample output files to validate parsers before integrating them into automation that drives decisions. This approach reduces errors and keeps your automation auditable and maintainable. These three core concepts are central to sustainable network automation with Python. First, virtual environments isolate dependencies and make your scripts reproducible across labs and CI systems. Second, netmiko builds on paramiko to simplify SSH-based CLI automation, providing helpers for send_command and send_config_set that abstract pagination and prompts. Third, always separate collection from parsing: capture raw show output to files and parse them later with libraries like TextFSM or genie. Keeping collection and parsing distinct reduces reconnects and lets you iterate on parsers without altering device runs. These concepts together form a practical foundation: reproducible environments, the right abstraction layer for SSH, and a disciplined two-step data flow that supports audits and iterative parser development.
